VIDEO.title: You Don't Understand Romans 5… And It's Affecting Your Gospel
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 5:1-11 · Episode 8 (#8 of 28 in the playlist)
hand: Justified, reconciled, and at peace with each other
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Romans 5:1-11. Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, access into grace, and hope of the glory of God (5:1-2). We boast even in afflictions, which bring perseverance, proven character and hope; hope does not put to shame, because God's love has been poured out within our hearts through the Holy Spirit (5:3-5). Christ died for the ungodly while we were still sinners; having been justified by His blood and reconciled while enemies, much more shall we be saved (5:6-11).

Paul builds on Romans 1-4: our righteous God makes a righteous people, Jew and Gentile together, by His faithfulness drawing out their faithful response. 5:1-2 forms a small chiasm with 'through our Lord Jesus Christ' at the center, and it rehearses 3:21-26: justification, faith, the glory of God.

'The glory of God' points to God's presence in the tabernacle and temple, the cloud the teacher calls the Shekinah (Exodus 16:10; 24:16-17; 40:34-38; 1 Kings 8:10-11). It departed in Ezekiel 10-11 and returned in the person of Jesus (John 1:14; Hebrews 1:3). Now all the justified have access.

Salvation in 5:9 echoes a new exodus: blood, wrath and deliverance, like Passover. At the Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus of His 'departure' (Luke 9:31). Paul argues 'much more' (5:9, 10), a rabbinic lesser-to-greater argument (qal vahomer).

Definitions: justification is God's covenant verdict declaring us in right standing with Him on the basis of faith in Christ; reconciliation is the restored relationship that verdict makes possible. In marriage terms, God says 'I do' first, while we were ungodly (4:5) and enemies (5:10), and faith is our 'I do.' Peace links to the covenant of peace (Numbers 25:12; Isaiah 54:10; Ezekiel 34:25), hope to Psalm 25:3 and the Greek of Isaiah 28:16, love poured out to Ezekiel 36 and Joel 2:28.

The lesson: 'Because God's people have peace and reconciliation with him, they must maintain peace and reconciliation with each other.' The passage is full of indicatives; as in Isaiah 54, they lead to a response (Matthew 5:9; Ephesians 4:1-3; Romans 12:18). The teacher recalls how most requests for his Debate Teacher Reacts videos were Christian against Christian.
QUOTES: Because God's people have peace and reconciliation with him, they must maintain peace and reconciliation with each other.
Justification is God's covenant verdict declaring us to be in right standing with him. Reconciliation is the renewed relationship that verdict makes possible.
The all-powerful God of the universe says, "I do" first.
If the realization of what God has done for us does not take your breath away, you've missed the message altogether.

method.p: Underline every statement of fact in Romans 5:1-11 (we have peace, we stand, we were reconciled). Then ask what response each fact invites. Compare Romans 12:18, an imperative built on these indicatives.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
“I will cut a covenant of peace with them and cause harmful beasts to cease from the land so that they may live securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.

src.text: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have obtained our introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we boast in hope of the glory of God.

lines.text: The teacher sees a thematic chiasm: justified by faith, peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ (the center), access into grace, hope of the glory of God. A covenant formula begins with justification and ends in the hope of glory, and it hinges on Jesus.
This rehashes 3:21-26: 'for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified as a gift by His grace' (Romans 3:23-24). Present access guarantees the final unveiling of God's glory.

left.text: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

right.text: “Then I will establish over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will shepherd them; he will shepherd them himself and be their shepherd. And I, Yahweh, will be their God, and My servant David will be prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken. “I will cut a covenant of peace with them and cause harmful beasts to cease from the land so that they may live securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.

lines.text: Paul links God's covenant declaration (justification) with shalom. God appoints the Messiah, the shepherd from David's line, and establishes a covenant of peace. Compare Numbers 25:12, Isaiah 26:3, 32:17, 54:10 and Psalm 85:8-10, where 'righteousness and peace have kissed each other.'

PEACE.title: Hope of the glory of God

left.text: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of Yahweh filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud had dwelt on it, and the glory of Yahweh filled the tabernacle.

right.text: And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, glory as of the only begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

lines.text: The glory of God is God's presence in the cloud: on Sinai (Exodus 24:16-17), in the tabernacle and in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11). It departed in Ezekiel 10-11 and returned in Jesus, 'the radiance of His glory' (Hebrews 1:3).
Instead of Moses or the high priest alone, everyone justified by faith now has access to that glory through Jesus.

left.text: And not only this, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction brings about perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope;

right.text: Yahweh is near to the brokenhearted / And saves those who are crushed in spirit.

lines.text: The Old Testament teaches that suffering is not wasted on God's people; it is an opportunity to cling to the Lord and learn from Him (Psalm 37:23-24; Proverbs 3:11-12).
Study note (added): James 1:2-4 traces the same chain: trials, testing, perseverance, maturity.

HOPE.title: Hope does not put to shame

left.text: and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out within our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.

right.text: Therefore thus says Lord Yahweh, / “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a tested stone, / A costly cornerstone for the foundation, firmly placed. / He who believes in it will not be disturbed.

lines.text: 'Let none who hope in You be ashamed' (Psalm 25:3). The teacher reads Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek Old Testament, where the one who believes in the cornerstone 'will not be put to shame'; Paul quotes that form in Romans 9:33 and 10:11.

left.text: “And it will be afterwards / That I will pour out My Spirit on all mankind; / And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; / Your old men will dream dreams; / Your young men will see visions.

right.text: “And I will pour out on the house of David and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and of supplication, so that they will look on Me whom they have pierced; and they will mourn for Him, as one mourns for an only son, and they will weep bitterly over Him like the bitter weeping over a firstborn.

lines.text: God putting something into our hearts echoes Ezekiel 36:26-27 (a new heart, My Spirit within you) and Joel 2. Zechariah links the pouring out of the Spirit with the one who was pierced.
Again Paul points to the source: the virtues of 5:3-4 rest on God's love poured out by the Holy Spirit.

left.text: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will hardly die for a righteous man, though perhaps for the good man someone would dare even to die. But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

right.text: Therefore, I will divide for Him a portion with the many, / And He will divide the spoil with the strong; / Because He poured out His soul to death, / And was numbered with the transgressors; / Yet He Himself bore the sin of many, / And interceded for the transgressors.

lines.text: 'Christ died for the ungodly' builds on 4:5, 'Him who justifies the ungodly.' It comes from Isaiah 53, where the Servant is pierced and crushed for transgressions and 'will justify the many' (Isaiah 53:11).

left.text: Much more then, having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from the wrath of God through Him.

right.text: And behold, two men were talking with Him, and they were Moses and Elijah, who, appearing in glory, were speaking of His departure which He was about to fulfill at Jerusalem.

lines.text: Salvation is deliverance, and the great deliverance is the exodus. Blood, wrath and salvation: Passover. Not out of Egypt this time, but out of sin and death. At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak of Jesus' departure, in Greek His exodus.

Paul argues from lesser to greater (qal vahomer): if justified by His blood, much more saved from wrath. The wrath echoes the prophets' day of the Lord (Nahum 1:2; Isaiah 13:9; Ezekiel 7:8; Zephaniah 1:18).

left.text: For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life. And not only this, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

right.text: For the mountains may be removed and the hills may shake, / But My lovingkindness will not be removed from you, / And My covenant of peace will not be shaken,” / Says Yahweh who has compassion on you.

lines.text: Justification is God's covenant verdict; reconciliation is the renewed relationship that verdict makes possible. Unlike a human marriage, God pursues a wayward people: 'your husband is your Maker' (Isaiah 54:5).
The response is subtle but unmistakable: 'the peace of your sons will be great' (Isaiah 54:13). God's people respond to His covenant of peace by making peace.

TERMS.def: God's covenant verdict declaring a person in right standing with Him on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ (video's definition; Romans 5:1).
God removing hostility and restoring relationship with former enemies through the death and life of Jesus (Romans 5:10-11).
Not only the end of hostility but wholeness and right relationship, the covenant of peace (Ezekiel 34:25).
God's manifest presence, seen in the cloud over tabernacle and temple and revealed in Jesus (John 1:14).
A rabbinic argument from lesser to greater: if this, then much more that (Romans 5:9-10).
Statements of fact (what God has done) and commands (what we must do); the first ground the second.
A mirrored structure (A-B-C-B-A) that points to its center (Romans 5:1-2).

BACKGROUND.h: 'We have peace' or 'let us have peace'?
BACKGROUND.p: Greek manuscripts of 5:1 differ by one letter: echomen ('we have') or echōmen ('let us have'). Many early manuscripts read 'let us have,' and Chrysostom preached on that reading; most modern translations, including the LSB, read 'we have' from the flow of the argument.

Shekinah ('dwelling') is a later rabbinic word for God's dwelling presence; it does not occur in the Old Testament, but it names what Exodus 40:34-35 describes: the cloud, and the glory filling the tabernacle.
The first of the seven rules of interpretation traditionally credited to Hillel: what holds in a lighter case holds all the more in a weightier one. Jesus uses it too ('how much more,' Matthew 7:11).
The LSB translates Luke 9:31 'His departure'; the Greek word is exodos. Luke frames Jesus' death and resurrection in Jerusalem as a new exodus.

DEBATES.h: 'We have peace' or 'let us have peace'?
DEBATES.p: The textual question in 5:1 (see Background). The video's lesson bridges both: we have peace with God, so we must keep peace with each other.

The video defines justification as God's covenant verdict of right standing. Reformation readings stress the legal verdict; some recent scholars stress covenant membership. The video combines the two.

DEBATES.h: Is there really a chiasm in 5:1-2?
DEBATES.p: Chiasms are common in Scripture, but scholars disagree on how many are intended. The video calls this one thematic; either way, Christ stands at the center of the sentence.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video cites Luke 9:29 for Moses and Elijah speaking of Jesus' departure; verse 29 is the change in His appearance, and the conversation is Luke 9:30-31.
The video reads 'rejoice' in Romans 5:2-3; the LSB has 'boast' (the same Greek verb as 'boasting' in 3:27, now turned toward God).
Isaiah 28:16 'will not be put to shame' is the Septuagint wording, as the video notes; the LSB, translating the Hebrew, reads 'will not be disturbed.'
The video says the glory departed 'never to return' to the holy of holies. Ezekiel 43:1-5 sees it return to a visionary temple; the video's point that it returned in Jesus stands.
'Shekinah' is a later rabbinic term; the Old Testament speaks of the cloud and the glory.

QUESTIONS: Which of the indicatives in Romans 5:1-11 do you find hardest to believe about yourself?
How do justification and reconciliation differ in the video's definitions?
What has affliction produced in you: perseverance, proven character, hope?
Where is God calling you to make peace with another believer?
Do your online habits look more like peacemaking or like the debates the teacher was asked to react to?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: Because God's people have peace and reconciliation with Him, they must maintain peace and reconciliation with each other. A newly married couple with every indicative in place (license, vows, cake) still has to go live in the reality of the new relationship. The teacher remembers starting Debate Teacher Reacts in August 2020 to smuggle apologetics training into reaction videos. He asked viewers which debates to react to next, and most suggestions were Christian against Christian. He calls that one of the biggest ways the church has conformed to the world: a lack of grace, mercy and compassion. As a new believer he brought his old argumentative habits with him, cheering the 'truth' half of Ephesians 4:15 and ignoring 'in love.' God loved us first while we were rebels. 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9).
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before you post or reply in a disagreement with another believer this week, read Romans 12:18 and Ephesians 4:3, and ask: will this keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace?

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Romans 5:1-11. Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, access into grace, and hope of the glory of God (5:1-2). We boast even in afflictions, which bring perseverance, proven character and hope; hope does not put to shame, because God's love has been poured out within our hearts through the Holy Spirit (5:3-5). Christ died for the ungodly while we were still sinners; having been justified by His blood and reconciled while enemies, much more shall we be saved (5:6-11).
- Paul builds on Romans 1-4: our righteous God makes a righteous people, Jew and Gentile together, by His faithfulness drawing out their faithful response. 5:1-2 forms a small chiasm with 'through our Lord Jesus Christ' at the center, and it rehearses 3:21-26: justification, faith, the glory of God.
- 'The glory of God' points to God's presence in the tabernacle and temple, the cloud the teacher calls the Shekinah (Exodus 16:10; 24:16-17; 40:34-38; 1 Kings 8:10-11). It departed in Ezekiel 10-11 and returned in the person of Jesus (John 1:14; Hebrews 1:3). Now all the justified have access.
- Salvation in 5:9 echoes a new exodus: blood, wrath and deliverance, like Passover. At the Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus of His 'departure' (Luke 9:31). Paul argues 'much more' (5:9, 10), a rabbinic lesser-to-greater argument (qal vahomer).
- Definitions: justification is God's covenant verdict declaring us in right standing with Him on the basis of faith in Christ; reconciliation is the restored relationship that verdict makes possible. In marriage terms, God says 'I do' first, while we were ungodly (4:5) and enemies (5:10), and faith is our 'I do.' Peace links to the covenant of peace (Numbers 25:12; Isaiah 54:10; Ezekiel 34:25), hope to Psalm 25:3 and the Greek of Isaiah 28:16, love poured out to Ezekiel 36 and Joel 2:28.
- The lesson: 'Because God's people have peace and reconciliation with him, they must maintain peace and reconciliation with each other.' The passage is full of indicatives; as in Isaiah 54, they lead to a response (Matthew 5:9; Ephesians 4:1-3; Romans 12:18). The teacher recalls how most requests for his Debate Teacher Reacts videos were Christian against Christian.

## Peace with God, access to glory
1. Romans 5:1-2: Christ at the center
   A small chiasm Romans 5:1-2: "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have obtained our introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we boast in hope of the glory of God." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+5:1-2
   (video) The teacher sees a thematic chiasm: justified by faith, peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ (the center), access into grace, hope of the glory of God. A covenant formula begins with justification and ends in the hope of glory, and it hinges on Jesus.
   (video) This rehashes 3:21-26: 'for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified as a gift by His grace' (Romans 3:23-24). Present access guarantees the final unveiling of God's glory. (Romans 3:21-26)
2. Romans 5:1; Ezekiel 34:23-25: A covenant of peace
   Paul (Romans 5:1, LSB): "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,"
   Ezekiel (Ezekiel 34:23-25, LSB): "“Then I will establish over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will shepherd them; he will shepherd them himself and be their shepherd. And I, Yahweh, will be their God, and My servant David will be prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken. “I will cut a covenant of peace with them and cause harmful beasts to cease from the land so that they may live securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods."
   (video) Paul links God's covenant declaration (justification) with shalom. God appoints the Messiah, the shepherd from David's line, and establishes a covenant of peace. Compare Numbers 25:12, Isaiah 26:3, 32:17, 54:10 and Psalm 85:8-10, where 'righteousness and peace have kissed each other.' (Numbers 25:12; Isaiah 32:17; Isaiah 54:10; Psalm 85:8-10)
3. Romans 5:2; Exodus 40:34-35: Hope of the glory of God
   Moses (Exodus 40:34-35, LSB): "Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of Yahweh filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud had dwelt on it, and the glory of Yahweh filled the tabernacle."
   John (John 1:14, LSB): "And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, glory as of the only begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth."
   (video) The glory of God is God's presence in the cloud: on Sinai (Exodus 24:16-17), in the tabernacle and in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11). It departed in Ezekiel 10-11 and returned in Jesus, 'the radiance of His glory' (Hebrews 1:3). (Exodus 24:16-17; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Ezekiel 10:18; Hebrews 1:3)
   (video) Instead of Moses or the high priest alone, everyone justified by faith now has access to that glory through Jesus.

## Hope that does not put to shame
1. Romans 5:3-4; Psalm 34:18: We boast in afflictions
   Paul (Romans 5:3-4, LSB): "And not only this, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction brings about perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope;"
   David (Psalm 34:18, LSB): "Yahweh is near to the brokenhearted / And saves those who are crushed in spirit."
   (video) The Old Testament teaches that suffering is not wasted on God's people; it is an opportunity to cling to the Lord and learn from Him (Psalm 37:23-24; Proverbs 3:11-12). (Psalm 37:23-24; Proverbs 3:11-12)
   [Background] Study note (added): James 1:2-4 traces the same chain: trials, testing, perseverance, maturity. (James 1:2-4)
2. Romans 5:5; Isaiah 28:16: Hope does not put to shame
   Paul (Romans 5:5, LSB): "and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out within our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us."
   Isaiah (Isaiah 28:16, LSB): "Therefore thus says Lord Yahweh, / “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a tested stone, / A costly cornerstone for the foundation, firmly placed. / He who believes in it will not be disturbed."
   (video) 'Let none who hope in You be ashamed' (Psalm 25:3). The teacher reads Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek Old Testament, where the one who believes in the cornerstone 'will not be put to shame'; Paul quotes that form in Romans 9:33 and 10:11. (Psalm 25:3; Romans 10:11)
3. Romans 5:5; Joel 2:28; Zechariah 12:10: Love poured out
   Joel (Joel 2:28, LSB): "“And it will be afterwards / That I will pour out My Spirit on all mankind; / And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; / Your old men will dream dreams; / Your young men will see visions."
   Zechariah (Zechariah 12:10, LSB): "“And I will pour out on the house of David and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and of supplication, so that they will look on Me whom they have pierced; and they will mourn for Him, as one mourns for an only son, and they will weep bitterly over Him like the bitter weeping over a firstborn."
   (video) God putting something into our hearts echoes Ezekiel 36:26-27 (a new heart, My Spirit within you) and Joel 2. Zechariah links the pouring out of the Spirit with the one who was pierced. (Ezekiel 36:26-27)
   (video) Again Paul points to the source: the virtues of 5:3-4 rest on God's love poured out by the Holy Spirit.

## Reconciled while enemies
1. Romans 5:6-8; Isaiah 53:12: While we were still sinners
   Paul (Romans 5:6-8, LSB): "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will hardly die for a righteous man, though perhaps for the good man someone would dare even to die. But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
   Isaiah (Isaiah 53:12, LSB): "Therefore, I will divide for Him a portion with the many, / And He will divide the spoil with the strong; / Because He poured out His soul to death, / And was numbered with the transgressors; / Yet He Himself bore the sin of many, / And interceded for the transgressors."
   (video) 'Christ died for the ungodly' builds on 4:5, 'Him who justifies the ungodly.' It comes from Isaiah 53, where the Servant is pierced and crushed for transgressions and 'will justify the many' (Isaiah 53:11). (Romans 4:5; Isaiah 53:11)
2. Romans 5:9; Luke 9:30-31: Much more: saved from wrath
   Paul (Romans 5:9, LSB): "Much more then, having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from the wrath of God through Him."
   Luke (Luke 9:30-31, LSB): "And behold, two men were talking with Him, and they were Moses and Elijah, who, appearing in glory, were speaking of His departure which He was about to fulfill at Jerusalem."
   (video) Salvation is deliverance, and the great deliverance is the exodus. Blood, wrath and salvation: Passover. Not out of Egypt this time, but out of sin and death. At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak of Jesus' departure, in Greek His exodus.
   (video) Paul argues from lesser to greater (qal vahomer): if justified by His blood, much more saved from wrath. The wrath echoes the prophets' day of the Lord (Nahum 1:2; Isaiah 13:9; Ezekiel 7:8; Zephaniah 1:18). (Zephaniah 1:18)
3. Romans 5:10-11; Isaiah 54:5, 10: Reconciled while enemies
   Paul (Romans 5:10-11, LSB): "For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life. And not only this, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation."
   Isaiah (Isaiah 54:10, LSB): "For the mountains may be removed and the hills may shake, / But My lovingkindness will not be removed from you, / And My covenant of peace will not be shaken,” / Says Yahweh who has compassion on you."
   (video) Justification is God's covenant verdict; reconciliation is the renewed relationship that verdict makes possible. Unlike a human marriage, God pursues a wayward people: 'your husband is your Maker' (Isaiah 54:5). (Isaiah 54:5)
   (video) The response is subtle but unmistakable: 'the peace of your sons will be great' (Isaiah 54:13). God's people respond to His covenant of peace by making peace. (Isaiah 54:13)

## Key people
- Paul: Explains how Romans 1-4 works out: through Christ's death and resurrection we are justified and reconciled. [Background] He calls it 'the ministry of reconciliation' in 2 Corinthians 5:18-19.
- Moses: Could not enter the tabernacle when the glory filled it; spoke with Jesus at the Transfiguration. [Background] Exodus 33:18-23: Moses asks, 'Show me Your glory.'
- Elijah: With Moses at the Transfiguration, speaking of Jesus' departure. [Background] Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah's return before the day of the Lord.
- Ezekiel: One shepherd, My servant David, and a covenant of peace (34:23-25); the glory departs (10-11). [Background] A priest-prophet in Babylonian exile.
- Joel and Zechariah: God pours out His Spirit (Joel 2:28); the Spirit of grace and the one pierced (Zechariah 12:10). [Background] Peter quotes Joel 2 at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21).
- Zephaniah: The day of the fury of Yahweh, against those who turned to other gods. [Background] Prophesied in the days of King Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1).

## Places [Background]
- Mount Sinai (named in the video): The glory of Yahweh dwelt on the mountain like a consuming fire (Exodus 24:16-17). Traditional site.
- Jerusalem (named in the video): The glory filled Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11); Jesus' departure was to be fulfilled here (Luke 9:31).
- Rome: The church Paul urges toward peace.
- Corinth: Where Paul probably wrote Romans.

## Key terms
- Justification: God's covenant verdict declaring a person in right standing with Him on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ (video's definition; Romans 5:1).
- Reconciliation: God removing hostility and restoring relationship with former enemies through the death and life of Jesus (Romans 5:10-11).
- Peace (shalom): Not only the end of hostility but wholeness and right relationship, the covenant of peace (Ezekiel 34:25).
- Glory of God: God's manifest presence, seen in the cloud over tabernacle and temple and revealed in Jesus (John 1:14).
- Qal vahomer: A rabbinic argument from lesser to greater: if this, then much more that (Romans 5:9-10).
- Indicative and imperative: Statements of fact (what God has done) and commands (what we must do); the first ground the second.
- Chiasm: A mirrored structure (A-B-C-B-A) that points to its center (Romans 5:1-2).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- 'We have peace' or 'let us have peace'?: Greek manuscripts of 5:1 differ by one letter: echomen ('we have') or echōmen ('let us have'). Many early manuscripts read 'let us have,' and Chrysostom preached on that reading; most modern translations, including the LSB, read 'we have' from the flow of the argument.
- Shekinah: Shekinah ('dwelling') is a later rabbinic word for God's dwelling presence; it does not occur in the Old Testament, but it names what Exodus 40:34-35 describes: the cloud, and the glory filling the tabernacle.
- Qal vahomer: The first of the seven rules of interpretation traditionally credited to Hillel: what holds in a lighter case holds all the more in a weightier one. Jesus uses it too ('how much more,' Matthew 7:11).
- Exodus, Luke 9:31: The LSB translates Luke 9:31 'His departure'; the Greek word is exodos. Luke frames Jesus' death and resurrection in Jerusalem as a new exodus.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- 'We have peace' or 'let us have peace'? The textual question in 5:1 (see Background). The video's lesson bridges both: we have peace with God, so we must keep peace with each other.
- Justification: verdict, covenant, or both? The video defines justification as God's covenant verdict of right standing. Reformation readings stress the legal verdict; some recent scholars stress covenant membership. The video combines the two.
- Is there really a chiasm in 5:1-2? Chiasms are common in Scripture, but scholars disagree on how many are intended. The video calls this one thematic; either way, Christ stands at the center of the sentence.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video cites Luke 9:29 for Moses and Elijah speaking of Jesus' departure; verse 29 is the change in His appearance, and the conversation is Luke 9:30-31.
- The video reads 'rejoice' in Romans 5:2-3; the LSB has 'boast' (the same Greek verb as 'boasting' in 3:27, now turned toward God).
- Isaiah 28:16 'will not be put to shame' is the Septuagint wording, as the video notes; the LSB, translating the Hebrew, reads 'will not be disturbed.'
- The video says the glory departed 'never to return' to the holy of holies. Ezekiel 43:1-5 sees it return to a visionary temple; the video's point that it returned in Jesus stands.
- 'Shekinah' is a later rabbinic term; the Old Testament speaks of the cloud and the glory.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Which of the indicatives in Romans 5:1-11 do you find hardest to believe about yourself?
2. How do justification and reconciliation differ in the video's definitions?
3. What has affliction produced in you: perseverance, proven character, hope?
4. Where is God calling you to make peace with another believer?
5. Do your online habits look more like peacemaking or like the debates the teacher was asked to react to?

## Application
- (video) Because God's people have peace and reconciliation with Him, they must maintain peace and reconciliation with each other. A newly married couple with every indicative in place (license, vows, cake) still has to go live in the reality of the new relationship. The teacher remembers starting Debate Teacher Reacts in August 2020 to smuggle apologetics training into reaction videos. He asked viewers which debates to react to next, and most suggestions were Christian against Christian. He calls that one of the biggest ways the church has conformed to the world: a lack of grace, mercy and compassion. As a new believer he brought his old argumentative habits with him, cheering the 'truth' half of Ephesians 4:15 and ignoring 'in love.' God loved us first while we were rebels. 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9).
- Study note (added): before you post or reply in a disagreement with another believer this week, read Romans 12:18 and Ephesians 4:3, and ask: will this keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace?
